blocks.md: A square matrix can be undone — inverted — only if it does not squash space flat. The determinant measures how much a matrix stretches or shrinks areas and volumes; if it is zero, the matrix collapses some direction to nothing, information is lost, and there is no way back. A whole list of conditions turns out to be the same thing: nonzero determinant, independent columns, full rank, no zero eigenvalue.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: In regression, whether the key matrix built from the data can be inverted decides whether the coefficients can be estimated at all.
For a square $n\times n$ matrix $A$, these statements are **all equivalent** — prove one and you have them all:

1. $A^{-1}$ exists
2. $\det(A) \neq 0$
3. $\mathrm{rank}(A) = n$ ([Linear Independence and Rank](note:linear-independence-and-rank))
4. The columns of $A$ are linearly independent
5. $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ only for $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$
6. No eigenvalue of $A$ is zero ([Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors](note:eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors))

For $2\times2$: $\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix} = ad - bc$. Geometrically, $|\det A|$ is the factor by which $A$ scales areas (volumes in higher dimensions); $\det A = 0$ means $A$ squashes space into a lower dimension, so the map cannot be undone.

| Property | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| Product | $\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)$ |
| Transpose | $\det(A') = \det(A)$ |
| Inverse | $\det(A^{-1}) = 1/\det(A)$ |
| Scalar | $\det(cA) = c^n\det(A)$ for $n\times n$ |
| Eigenvalues | $\det(A) = \prod_i \lambda_i$ |
| Triangular | Product of the diagonal |

$\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\4&2\end{pmatrix}$: $\det = 4 - 4 = 0$. The second column is half the first, so the columns are dependent and there is no inverse. $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$: $\det = -2 \neq 0$, invertible.

- Only square matrices have determinants or inverses. A non-square $\mathbf{X}$ is handled through the square $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}$.
- $\det(A + B) \neq \det(A) + \det(B)$.

- **Econometrics**: $(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ exists exactly when $\mathbf{X}$ has full column rank — [Full Rank and Identification](note:full-rank-and-identification); the dummy variable trap in [Indicator Variables](note:indicator-variables) is a singular $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}$.
- **Probability**: the Jacobian determinant in [Change of Variables](note:change-of-variables).
